claim: Catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs) account for 40% of all hospital-acquired infections.
source: The most common complication is catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI), which accounts for 40% of all hospital-acquired infections (Andersen and Flores-Mireles, 2019; Feneley et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Andersen and Flores-Mireles, 2019; Feneley et al., 2015).

claim: CAUTIs often lead to bloodstream infections and systemic dissemination with a 30% mortality rate.
source: Unfortunately, CAUTIs often lead to bloodstream infections and systemic dissemination with a 30% mortality rate, causing significant financial burdens for hospitals and patients (Andersen and Flores-Mireles, 2019; Feneley et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Andersen and Flores-Mireles, 2019; Feneley et al., 2015).

claim: Catheter use elicits bladder inflammation, releasing host serum proteins, including fibrinogen (Fg), into the bladder.
source: Catheter use elicits bladder inflammation, releasing host serum proteins, including fibrinogen (Fg), into the bladder, which deposit on the urinary catheter.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about catheter-induced inflammation and is referenced in the context of the study's findings.

claim: Enterococcus faecalis uses fibrinogen as a scaffold to bind and persist in the bladder despite antibiotic treatments.
source: Enterococcus faecalis uses Fg as a scaffold to bind and persist in the bladder despite antibiotic treatments.
evidence: The claim is supported by prior research findings cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: Inhibition of fibrinogen-pathogen interaction significantly reduces infection.
source: Inhibition of Fg–pathogen interaction significantly reduces infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by prior research findings and is a key premise of the study.

claim: Deposited fibrinogen is advantageous for uropathogens E. faecalis, Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, K. pneumoniae, A. baumannii, and C. albicans.
source: Here, we show deposited Fg is advantageous for uropathogens E. faecalis, Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, K. pneumoniae, A. baumannii, and C. albicans, suggesting that targeting catheter protein deposition may reduce colonization creating an effective intervention for catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing pathogen-fibrinogen interactions.

claim: Liquid-infused silicone catheters reduce host-protein deposition in a mouse model of CAUTI.
source: In a mouse model of CAUTI, host-protein deposition was reduced, using liquid-infused silicone catheters, resulting in decreased colonization on catheters, in bladders, and dissemination in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the mouse CAUTI model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Liquid-infused silicone catheters result in decreased colonization on catheters and in bladders in vivo.
source: In a mouse model of CAUTI, host-protein deposition was reduced, using liquid-infused silicone catheters, resulting in decreased colonization on catheters, in bladders, and dissemination in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the mouse CAUTI model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Liquid-infused silicone catheters reduce dissemination of pathogens in vivo.
source: In a mouse model of CAUTI, host-protein deposition was reduced, using liquid-infused silicone catheters, resulting in decreased colonization on catheters, in bladders, and dissemination in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the mouse CAUTI model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Proteomics revealed a significant decrease in deposition of host-secreted proteins on liquid-infused catheter surfaces.
source: Furthermore, proteomics revealed a significant decrease in deposition of host-secreted proteins on liquid-infused catheter surfaces.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: All tested uropathogens colocalize strongly with fibrinogen deposits on catheters in vivo.
source: Visual and quantitative analysis of the catheters showed all uropathogens colocalizing strongly with Fg deposits exhibiting preference for Fg (Figure 1A, B) and robust Fg deposition on catheters, validating previous studies on human catheters (Flores-Mireles et al., 2019; Flores-Mireles et al., 2014; Flores-Mireles et al., 2016a; Flores-Mireles et al., 2016b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 1A, B.

claim: All tested uropathogens interact with fibrinogen on the bladder urothelium or in the lumen during CAUTI.
source: Importantly, immunofluorescence (IF) analysis of bladder sections showed that all uropathogens interact with Fg on the bladder urothelium or in the lumen during CAUTI (Figure 1C and montages in Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence analysis of bladder sections shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fibrinogen significantly enhances uropathogen binding to silicone catheters compared with uncoated and BSA-coated silicone catheters.
source: We compared uropathogen binding to Fg-, BSA-, and uncoated silicone, finding that Fg significantly enhanced the binding to the catheter for all uropathogens when compared with uncoated and BSA-coated silicone catheters (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 2.

claim: P. aeruginosa binding to BSA-coated silicone was ~14% higher than uncoated controls.
source: Interestingly, P. aeruginosa and A. baumannii binding to BSA-coated silicone was ~14% and ~10% higher than uncoated controls, respectively (Figure 2C, E), alluding to a role for other host-secreted proteins during infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative binding assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A. baumannii binding to BSA-coated silicone was ~10% higher than uncoated controls.
source: Interestingly, P. aeruginosa and A. baumannii binding to BSA-coated silicone was ~14% and ~10% higher than uncoated controls, respectively (Figure 2C, E), alluding to a role for other host-secreted proteins during infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative binding assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Fibrinogen is continuously released into the bladder lumen in response to mechanical damage to the urothelial lining caused by catheterization.
source: Fg is continuously released into the bladder lumen in response to mechanical damage to the urothelial lining caused by catheterization (Flores-Mireles et al., 2019; Flores-Mireles et al., 2014; Flores-Mireles et al., 2016a; Klein and Hultgren, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Flores-Mireles et al., 2019; Flores-Mireles et al., 2014; Flores-Mireles et al., 2016a; Klein and Hultgren, 2020).

claim: When blocking the interaction between fibrinogen and E. faecalis using antibodies, the pathogen is not able to effectively colonize the bladder.
source: When blocking the interaction between Fg and E. faecalis using antibodies, the pathogen is not able to effectively colonize the bladder (Di Venanzio et al., 2019; Flores-Mireles et al., 2014; Flores-Mireles et al., 2016a; Gaston et al., 2020; Walker et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Di Venanzio et al., 2019; Flores-Mireles et al., 2014; Flores-Mireles et al., 2016a; Gaston et al., 2020; Walker et al., 2017).

claim: Liquid-infused silicone (LIS) is more simple to make, more stable, and more cost effective than other antifouling polymer modifications.
source: LIS is more simple to make, more stable, and more cost effective than other antifouling polymer modifications (Andersen and Flores-Mireles, 2019; Campoccia et al., 2013; Homeyer et al., 2019; Howell et al., 2018; Chamy, 2013; Singha et al., 2017; Sotiri et al., 2018; Villegas et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature comparing different antifouling modifications.

claim: LIS has shown to reduce clotting in central lines and infection in skin implants.
source: Additionally, LIS has shown to reduce clotting in central lines and infection in skin implants (Chen et al., 2017; Leslie et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Chen et al., 2017; Leslie et al., 2014).

claim: LIS-catheters reduced fibrinogen deposition and microbial binding in vitro.
source: We show that our LIS-catheters reduced Fg deposition and microbial binding not only in vitro but also in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: LIS-catheters reduced fibrinogen deposition and microbial binding in vivo.
source: We show that our LIS-catheters reduced Fg deposition and microbial binding not only in vitro but also in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo experimental data from the mouse CAUTI model.

claim: LIS-catheters significantly decrease host-protein deposition when compared to unmodified catheters.
source: Furthermore, LIS-catheters significantly decrease host-protein deposition when compared to unmodified (UM)-catheters as well as reducing catheter-induced inflammation.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: LIS-catheters reduce catheter-induced inflammation.
source: Furthermore, LIS-catheters significantly decrease host-protein deposition when compared to unmodified (UM)-catheters as well as reducing catheter-induced inflammation.
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Catheters impregnated with antimicrobials have shown, at best, mixed results in clinical trials.
source: Catheters impregnated with antimicrobials, such as metal ions and antibiotics, have become popular and are now commercialized due to promising in vitro work but, in clinical trials these catheters have shown, at best, mixed results (Andersen and Flores-Mireles, 2019; Singha et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Andersen and Flores-Mireles, 2019; Singha et al., 2017).

claim: The presence of antimicrobial compounds on catheters may drive development of resistance.
source: Importantly, there is concern that this approach may not be a long-term solution given that the presence of antimicrobial compounds may drive development of resistance (Singha et al., 2017; Westfall et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Singha et al., 2017; Westfall et al., 2019).

claim: Fibrinogen deposition was reduced by ~90% on Dover LIS-catheters compared to unmodified controls.
source: We found that Fg deposition was reduced in all LIS-catheters, showing ~90% decrease on Dover and ~100% on the Bardex and medical-grade silicone tubing when compared with the corresponding UM controls (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 3A, B.

claim: Fibrinogen deposition was reduced by ~100% on Bardex LIS-catheters compared to unmodified controls.
source: We found that Fg deposition was reduced in all LIS-catheters, showing ~90% decrease on Dover and ~100% on the Bardex and medical-grade silicone tubing when compared with the corresponding UM controls (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 3A, B.

claim: Fibrinogen deposition was reduced by ~100% on medical-grade silicone LIS-tubing compared to unmodified controls.
source: We found that Fg deposition was reduced in all LIS-catheters, showing ~90% decrease on Dover and ~100% on the Bardex and medical-grade silicone tubing when compared with the corresponding UM controls (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 3A, B.

claim: All tested uropathogens bound in significantly higher densities to unmodified catheters than to LIS-catheters.
source: Binding analysis by each of the uropathogens showed that all were able to bind in significantly higher densities to the UM-catheters than to the LIS-catheters (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Mice with LIS-catheters had significantly reduced microbial colonization in the bladder compared with UM-catheterized mice regardless of the infecting uropathogen.
source: We found that mice with LIS-catheters significantly reduced microbial colonization in the bladder and on catheters when compared with UM-catheterized mice regardless of the infecting uropathogen (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU enumeration data from the mouse CAUTI model shown in Figure 4.

claim: Mice with LIS-catheters had significantly reduced microbial colonization on catheters compared with UM-catheterized mice regardless of the infecting uropathogen.
source: We found that mice with LIS-catheters significantly reduced microbial colonization in the bladder and on catheters when compared with UM-catheterized mice regardless of the infecting uropathogen (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU enumeration data from the mouse CAUTI model shown in Figure 4.

claim: Colonization was significantly lower in LIS-catheterized mouse kidneys for P. aeruginosa, A. baumannii, and E. coli infections.
source: Additionally, colonization was significantly lower in LIS-catheterized mouse kidneys for P. aeruginosa, A. baumannii, and E. coli infections (Figure 4C, E, G) and LIS-catheterized mice infected with E. coli or C. albicans showed significantly less colonization of the spleen (Figure 4G, K).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU enumeration data from kidneys shown in Figure 4C, E, G.

claim: LIS-catheterized mice infected with E. coli or C. albicans showed significantly less colonization of the spleen.
source: Additionally, colonization was significantly lower in LIS-catheterized mouse kidneys for P. aeruginosa, A. baumannii, and E. coli infections (Figure 4C, E, G) and LIS-catheterized mice infected with E. coli or C. albicans showed significantly less colonization of the spleen (Figure 4G, K).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU enumeration data from spleens shown in Figure 4G, K.

claim: K. pneumoniae-infected mice with LIS-catheters showed significantly less colonization of the heart.
source: K. pneumoniae kidney and spleen colonization difference was not statistically significant, however they showed a trend of less colonization and there was significantly less colonization of the heart (Figure 4I).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU enumeration data from hearts shown in Figure 4I.

claim: The LIS-catheter does not exacerbate bladder inflammation regardless of the presence of infection or not.
source: Importantly, hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) analysis shows the LI-catheter does not exacerbate bladder inflammation regardless of the presence of infection or not (Figure 5A–G), an important factor to account for when developing a new medical device.
evidence: The claim is supported by H&E histological analysis shown in Figure 5A–G.

claim: For some pathogens, the LIS-catheter results in less inflammation than bladders catheterized with an unmodified catheter.
source: In fact, for some pathogens, the LI-catheter results in less inflammation than bladders catheterized with an UM-catheter (Figure 5B, C, G).
evidence: The claim is supported by H&E histological analysis shown in Figure 5B, C, G.

claim: LIS-catheterized and infected bladders show a reduction of microbial colonization and decreased neutrophil recruitment.
source: Furthermore, we examine Fg presence, uropathogen colonization, and neutrophil recruitment in UM- and LIS-catheterized and infected bladders by IF microscopy. This analysis revealed a reduction of microbial colonization as well as decreased neutrophil recruitment (Figure 5H–M).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5H–M.

claim: Total abundance of protein was significantly reduced in LIS- vs UM-catheters.
source: Total abundance of protein was significantly reduced in LIS- vs UM-catheters (Figure 6A and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative proteomics data shown in Figure 6A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Abundance of fibrinogen and over 130 other proteins significantly decreased on LIS-catheters compared to UM-catheters.
source: Additionally, abundance of Fg and over 130 other proteins significantly decreased while only three proteins showed a significant increase (UDP-glucose 6-dehydrogenase, filamin-B, and proteasome subunit beta type-5) (Figure 6B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative proteomics data shown in Figure 6B and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Only three proteins showed a significant increase on LIS-catheters: UDP-glucose 6-dehydrogenase, filamin-B, and proteasome subunit beta type-5.
source: Additionally, abundance of Fg and over 130 other proteins significantly decreased while only three proteins showed a significant increase (UDP-glucose 6-dehydrogenase, filamin-B, and proteasome subunit beta type-5) (Figure 6B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative proteomics data shown in Figure 6B and Supplementary file 2.

claim: 865 proteins were identified at a 1% False Discovery Rate (FDR) in the proteomic analysis.
source: nLC–MS/MS was performed in technical duplicate and label-free-proteomics (LFQ) processed as in Cox and Mann, 865 proteins were identified at a 1% False Discovery Rate (FDR) (Cox and Mann, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data analysis described in the methods.

claim: Silicone weight increased significantly during the first 3 days of infusion then gradually decreased until a plateau was reached after ~50 hr.
source: Analysis of the oil's infusion rate showed a significant increase in silicone weight during the first 3 days of infusion then a gradual decrease in infusion until a plateau was reached after ~50 hr (raw weight in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by weight measurement data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Full infusion of mouse silicone catheters was achieved by 10 min of infusion.
source: Full infusion of mouse silicone catheters was achieved by 10 min of infusion (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by weight measurement data shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Silicone tube dimensions showed an increase in length by ~41.3%, outer diameter by ~103.1%, and inner diameter by ~27.6% after infusion.
source: Investigation of silicone tube dimensions showed an increase in length, outer diameter, and inner diameter of ~41.3%, ~ 103.1%, and ~27.6%, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) and mouse catheters showed an increase of ~30.7%, ~28.7%, and ~39.8%, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by dimensional measurement data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Mouse catheters showed an increase in length by ~30.7%, outer diameter by ~28.7%, and inner diameter by ~39.8% after infusion.
source: Investigation of silicone tube dimensions showed an increase in length, outer diameter, and inner diameter of ~41.3%, ~ 103.1%, and ~27.6%, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) and mouse catheters showed an increase of ~30.7%, ~28.7%, and ~39.8%, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by dimensional measurement data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The mouse model of CAUTI faithfully recapitulates the pathophysiology of human CAUTI.
source: Our mouse model of CAUTI has shown to faithfully recapitulate the pathophysiology of human CAUTI, showing urinary catheterization induces inflammation and contribution of Fg to biofilm formation on catheters recovered from humans suffering of CAUTI (Delnay et al., 1999; Flores-Mireles et al., 2014; Flores-Mireles et al., 2016a; Flores-Mireles et al., 2016b; Glahn et al., 1988; Peychl and Zalud, 2008; Walker et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature comparing mouse and human CAUTI pathophysiology.

claim: Fibrinogen is highly glycosylated, containing a wide variety of sugar residues including mannose, N-acetyl glucosamine, fucose, galactose, and N‐acetylneuraminic acid.
source: Interestingly, Fg is highly glycosylated, containing a wide variety of sugar residues including mannose, N-acetyl glucosamine, fucose, galactose, and N‐acetylneuraminic acid (Adamczyk et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Adamczyk et al., 2013).

claim: The glycosylation in fibrinogen may be recognized by CUP pili, allowing pathogens expressing CUP adhesins to become established and colonize the bladder.
source: Interestingly, Fg is highly glycosylated, containing a wide variety of sugar residues including mannose, N-acetyl glucosamine, fucose, galactose, and N‐acetylneuraminic acid (Adamczyk et al., 2013). Therefore, the glycosylation in Fg may be recognized by CUP pili, allowing pathogens expressing CPU adhesins to become established and colonize the bladder.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the glycosylation of fibrinogen and known CUP pili binding specificities.

claim: A. baumannii CUP1 and CUP2 pili are essential for CAUTI.
source: Furthermore, A. baumannii CUP1 and CUP2 pili are essential for CAUTI, this together with A. baumannii interactions with Fg in vivo, suggests that these pili may play a role in Fg interaction (Di Venanzio et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Di Venanzio et al., 2019).

claim: A. baumannii CUP1 and CUP2 pili may play a role in fibrinogen interaction.
source: Furthermore, A. baumannii CUP1 and CUP2 pili are essential for CAUTI, this together with A. baumannii interactions with Fg in vivo, suggests that these pili may play a role in Fg interaction (Di Venanzio et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the essentiality of CUP pili for CAUTI and observed Fg interactions.

claim: C. albicans has several adhesins, ALS1, ALS3, and ALS9, which have a conserved peptide-binding cavity shown to bind to fibrinogen γ-chain.
source: Furthermore, C. albicans has several adhesins, ALS1, ALS3, and ALS9, which have a conserved peptide-binding cavity shown to bind to Fg γ-chain (Hoyer and Cota, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Hoyer and Cota, 2016).

claim: In vitro studies do not efficiently mimic the complexities of the in vivo environment.
source: It is possible that in vitro studies do not efficiently mimic the complexities of the in vivo environment, for example; (1) Growth media: the majority of in vitro studies use laboratory rich or defined culture media, and it has been shown that laboratory media do not recapitulate the catheterized bladder environment that pathogens encounter (Colomer-Winter et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Colomer-Winter et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2017).

claim: Laboratory media do not recapitulate the catheterized bladder environment that pathogens encounter.
source: It is possible that in vitro studies do not efficiently mimic the complexities of the in vivo environment, for example; (1) Growth media: the majority of in vitro studies use laboratory rich or defined culture media, and it has been shown that laboratory media do not recapitulate the catheterized bladder environment that pathogens encounter (Colomer-Winter et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Colomer-Winter et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2017).

claim: Urine culture conditions activate different bacterial transcriptional profiles than when cultures are grown in defined media.
source: Specifically, urine culture conditions have shown to activate different bacterial transcriptional profiles than when cultures are grown in defined media (Conover et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2017), which may affect microbial persistence and survival.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Conover et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2017).

claim: Host-protein deposition on catheters is not uniform.
source: As has been observed with Fg deposition on human and mouse catheters, that host-protein deposition is not uniform, which may lead to antimicrobial release or pathogen–antimicrobial agent interaction at a subinhibitory concentrations (Di Venanzio et al., 2019; Flores-Mireles et al., 2014; Flores-Mireles et al., 2016a; Walker et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Di Venanzio et al., 2019; Flores-Mireles et al., 2014; Flores-Mireles et al., 2016a; Walker et al., 2017).

claim: Non-uniform host-protein deposition may lead to antimicrobial release or pathogen-antimicrobial agent interaction at subinhibitory concentrations.
source: As has been observed with Fg deposition on human and mouse catheters, that host-protein deposition is not uniform, which may lead to antimicrobial release or pathogen–antimicrobial agent interaction at a subinhibitory concentrations (Di Venanzio et al., 2019; Flores-Mireles et al., 2014; Flores-Mireles et al., 2016a; Walker et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from non-uniform protein deposition and its potential effects on antimicrobial efficacy.

claim: Subinhibitory concentrations of antimicrobials can contribute to the development of multidrug resistance among uropathogens.
source: Consequently, these interactions can contribute to the development of multidrug resistance among uropathogens ('Antibiotic resistance threats in the Antibiotic resistance threats in the United States, 2019', 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on inference and supported by a citation to a report on antibiotic resistance threats.

claim: Antifouling catheter coatings present a better approach to decreasing CAUTI prevalence than using biocidal or biostatic compounds that promote resistance.
source: Based on the role of deposited host proteins in promoting microbial colonization and presence in human CAUTI (Flores-Mireles et al., 2016a; Flores-Mireles et al., 2016b; Walker et al., 2017), antifouling catheter coatings present a better approach to decreasing CAUTI prevalence rather than using biocidal or biostatic compounds, such as antibiotics, that promote resistance (Campoccia et al., 2013; Singha et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the role of host proteins and is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Antifouling coatings made from polymers have shown resistance to protein deposition.
source: Antifouling coatings made from polymers have shown resistance to protein deposition He et al., 2016; however, these coatings can become unstable over time and be difficult to produce requiring extensive wet chemistry (Singha et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (He et al., 2016; Singha et al., 2017).

claim: Polymer antifouling coatings can become unstable over time and be difficult to produce requiring extensive wet chemistry.
source: Antifouling coatings made from polymers have shown resistance to protein deposition He et al., 2016; however, these coatings can become unstable over time and be difficult to produce requiring extensive wet chemistry (Singha et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Singha et al., 2017).

claim: Most reports on the use of purely antifouling coatings to combat CAUTI have shown a successful reduction in bacterial colonization in vitro yet have not been successfully tested in vivo.
source: Most reports on the use of purely antifouling coatings to combat CAUTI have shown a successful reduction in bacterial colonization in vitro yet have not been successfully tested in vivo (Andersen and Flores-Mireles, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Andersen and Flores-Mireles, 2019).

claim: Many antifouling coatings are optimized to target bacterial adhesion as the first stage of biofilm development.
source: This may be partly explained by the fact that many of the antifouling coatings are optimized to target bacterial adhesion, as it is understood that the first stage of biofilm development is bacterial attachment to a surface (Faustino et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Faustino et al., 2020).

claim: In the in vivo bladder environment, the first change to the catheter surface is the adhesion of a complex set of host-generated proteins and biological molecules (conditioning film).
source: However, in a complex environment such as the in vivo bladder, the first change to the catheter surface is the adhesion of a complex set of host-generated proteins and biological molecules, generally referred to as a conditioning film, which can mask the surface (Faustino et al., 2020; Gaston et al., 2020; Scotland et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Faustino et al., 2020; Gaston et al., 2020; Scotland et al., 2020).

claim: Studies on catheter coatings to-date have rarely focused on the role of host-secreted proteins.
source: Yet studies on catheter coatings to-date have rarely focused on the role of the host in infection establishment; namely, the host-secreted proteins.
evidence: The claim is based on a review of the literature and represents a gap in the field.

claim: The missing element of host-secreted proteins may partly explain the differing results seen for most antifouling catheter treatments in vitro vs in vivo.
source: The data we present here suggest that this missing element may at least partly explain the differing results seen for most antifouling catheter treatments in vitro vs in vivo.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study's findings about the importance of host proteins.

claim: The use of a liquid surface may convey additional anti-inflammatory benefits.
source: This findings are consistent with previous a in vivo work showing reduced fibrous capsule formation in implants coated with a liquid layer, suggesting that the use of a liquid surface may convey additional anti-inflammatory benefits (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from prior work and is supported by a citation (Chen et al., 2017).

claim: The deposition of host-secreted proteins on LIS-catheters was around 6.5-fold less than UM-catheters.
source: Finally, the deposition of other host-secreted proteins on LIS-catheters was around 6.5-fold less then UM-catheters.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: LIS-catheters are a promising new antibiotic-sparing approach for reducing or preventing CAUTIs by interfering with protein deposition.
source: Together, these findings indicate that catheters made using LIS are a promising new antibiotic sparring approach for reducing or even preventing CAUTIs by interfering with protein deposition (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is based on the cumulative findings of the study and represents the main conclusion.

claim: Serum albumin is one of the most abundant proteins on human and mouse urinary catheters.
source: In addition to Fg, bovine serum albumin (BSA) was tested since serum albumin is one of the most abundant proteins on human and mouse urinary catheters (Molina et al., in preparation; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from an in-preparation manuscript and supplementary data.
